paras.text: Topic: 喜好 Hobbies
• Learning to describe likes/dislikes (e.g., sports and movies).
• Learning to express what two groups have in common.
• Learning to politely ask others their opinions and make simple suggestions.
• Learning to form choice questions.

lines.py: Tiánzhōng, nǐ xǐhuān tīng yīnyuè ma?

lines.zh: 我不喜歡聽音樂。我喜歡運動。
lines.py: Wǒ bù xǐhuān tīng yīnyuè. Wǒ xǐhuān yùndòng.
Dǎ bàngqiú hàn yóuyǒng, nǐ ne?

lines.zh: 我常打籃球，也常踢足球。
lines.py: Wǒ cháng dǎ lánqiú, yě cháng tī zúqiú.
Wǒ juéde tī zúqiú hěn hǎowán.

lines.zh: 明天是週末，我們早上去踢足球，怎麼樣？
lines.py: Míngtiān shì zhōumò. Wǒmen zǎoshàng qù tī zúqiú, zěnmeyàng?

translation.en: Tianzhong, do you like listening to music?
I don't like listening to music. I like to exercise.
Do you like to play tennis?
I don't like to play tennis.
What do you like to do?
Play baseball and swim. And you?
I often play basketball and also often play soccer.
The weekend is tomorrow. How about we go play soccer tomorrow morning?

items.en: How about it? How does that sound? What do you think?

lines.zh: 今天晚上我們去看電影，好不好？
lines.py: Jīntiān wǎnshàng wǒmen qù kàn diànyǐng, hǎo bù hǎo?

lines.zh: 妳想看美國電影還是臺灣電影？
lines.py: Nǐ xiǎng kàn Měiguó diànyǐng háishì Táiwān diànyǐng?

lines.zh: 美國電影、臺灣電影，我都想看。
lines.py: Měiguó diànyǐng, Táiwān diànyǐng, wǒ dōu xiǎng kàn.

lines.zh: 好啊！看電影可以學中文。
lines.py: Hǎo a! Kàn diànyǐng kěyǐ xué Zhōngwén.

lines.zh: 晚上要不要一起吃晚飯？
lines.py: Wǎnshàng yào bú yào yìqǐ chī wǎnfàn?
Hǎo, wǒmen qù chī Yuènán cài.

translation.en: Let's go see a movie tonight, OK?
Do you want to see an American movie or a Taiwanese movie?
Either an American movie or a Taiwanese film is fine with me.
Let's go ahead and see a Taiwanese movie.
That's fine. Watching movies, I can learn Chinese.
Would you like to have dinner together tonight?
Okay. Let's go have Vietnamese food.

items.en: How about...? How does that sound?

paras.text: Structures: Time words appear after (mostly) or before (less commonly) the subject.

items.en: We went to see a movie today.

items.py: Nǐ míngtiān xiǎng qù yóuyǒng ma?
items.en: Would you like to go swimming tomorrow?

items.py: Zhōumò tā yào qù dǎ lánqiú.
items.en: This weekend, he is going to go play basketball.
What would you like to do tomorrow?

paras.text: Usage: Units of time in a series are expressed from larger to smaller. For example,
1. 明天晚上 míngtiān wǎnshàng (tomorrow evening) — not *晚上明天
2. 週末早上 zhōumò zǎoshàng (in the morning on the weekend) — not *早上週末

blocks.en: II. To Go Do Something with 去 qù

paras.text: Function: 去 qù + VP indicates the intention to go do something.

items.en: I am going to go play tennis.

items.zh: 我們和老師都去看電影。
items.py: Wǒmen hàn lǎoshī dōu qù kàn diànyǐng.
items.en: We and the teacher are all going to go see a movie.

paras.text: Structures: Negation markers, auxiliary verbs, and adverbs are placed before 去 qù.

items.en: I am not going to go play basketball.

items.py: Míngtiān zǎoshàng wǒ bú qù yóuyǒng.
items.en: I am not going to go swimming tomorrow morning.

items.py: Nǐ yào qù kàn diànyǐng ma?
items.en: Would you like to go see a movie?

items.py: Nǐmen cháng qù chī Yuènán cài ma?
items.en: Do you often go eat Vietnamese food?

items.py: Tā bú qù dǎ bàngqiú ma?
items.en: Is he not going to go play baseball?

paras.text: Function: When you want to describe, explain, or evaluate a person, event, or thing, you place the person, event, or thing at the beginning of the sentence as the “topic”. The rest of the sentence serves as the “comment”. The topic of a sentence is usually the person or thing that is placed at the beginning of the sentence.

a.zh: 臺灣人喜歡喝烏龍茶嗎？
a.py: Táiwān rén xǐhuān hē Wūlóng chá ma?
a.en: Do Taiwanese people like to drink Oolong tea?

b.zh: 烏龍茶，臺灣人都喜歡喝。
b.py: Wūlóng chá, Táiwān rén dōu xǐhuān hē.
b.en: Oolong tea, Taiwanese people all like to drink (it).

a.en: Do you have any brothers and sisters?

a.zh: 你想看美國電影還是臺灣電影？
a.py: Nǐ xiǎng kàn Měiguó diànyǐng háishì Táiwān diànyǐng?
a.en: Do you want to watch an American movie or a Taiwanese movie?

b.zh: 美國電影、臺灣電影，我都想看。
b.py: Měiguó diànyǐng, Táiwān diànyǐng, wǒ dōu xiǎng kàn.
b.en: American movie, Taiwanese movie, I would like to watch either.

paras.text: Structures: Topics are always placed at the very beginning of a sentence.

items.zh: 這張照片，我覺得很好看。
items.py: Zhè zhāng zhàopiàn, wǒ juéde hěn hǎokàn.
items.en: This photo, I think (it) is quite nice.

paras.text: Usage: In a topic-comment sentence, if the fronted object consists of a collective noun, or more than one noun, the totality marker, 都 dōu is required.

items.zh: 中國菜，我都喜歡吃。（collective noun）
items.py: Zhōngguó cài, wǒ dōu xǐhuān chī.
items.en: Chinese food, I like to eat (them) all.

items.zh: 弟弟、妹妹，我都有。（two object nouns）
items.en: Younger brothers and younger sisters, I've got both.

items.prompt: 我常看美國電影。 → ＿＿＿＿＿＿，我常看。
我覺得踢足球很好玩。 → ＿＿＿＿＿＿，我覺得很好玩。
A：你喜歡喝臺灣茶還是日本茶？　B：＿＿＿茶、＿＿＿茶，我都不喝。
A：你喜歡越南菜還是臺灣菜？　B：＿＿＿和＿＿＿，我＿＿＿＿＿＿。
A：你有弟弟和妹妹嗎？　B：＿＿＿和＿＿＿，我＿＿＿＿＿＿。
A：網球、籃球，你都喜歡嗎？　B：＿＿＿，我喜歡；＿＿＿，我＿＿＿＿＿＿。

blocks.en: IV. The Word Order of Adverbs 也 yě, 都 dōu and 常 cháng

paras.text: Structures:
1. 也 yě, 都 dōu and 常 cháng are adverbs. Adverbs modify verbs. Adverbs always occur before the verb in Chinese.
也 yě／都 dōu／常 cháng + VP
2. When 也 yě and either 都 dōu or 常 cháng occur in a sentence together to modify the VP, 也 yě is placed before 都 dōu or 常 cháng.
Negation: In negation, 也 yě is placed before the negation markers 不 bù／沒 méi, while 常 cháng is placed after 不 bù. 都 dōu can occur before or after 不 bù, but it changes the meaning of the sentence.

items.zh: 我不是日本人，他也不是日本人。
items.py: Wǒ bú shì Rìběn rén, tā yě bú shì Rìběn rén.
items.en: I am not Japanese and he is not, either.

items.zh: 我沒有弟弟，也沒有妹妹。
items.py: Wǒ méi yǒu dìdi, yě méi yǒu mèimei.
items.en: I don't have a younger brother or a younger sister.

items.zh: 他不喜歡看電影，我也不喜歡看電影。
items.py: Tā bù xǐhuān kàn diànyǐng, wǒ yě bù xǐhuān kàn diànyǐng.
items.en: He doesn't like to watch movies and I don't like to watch movies, either.

items.py: Wǒmen dōu bú shì Měiguó rén.

items.zh: 他們不都是美國人。（有美國人，也有日本人）
items.py: Tāmen bù dōu shì Měiguó rén. (Yǒu Měiguó rén, yě yǒu Rìběn rén.)
items.en: Not all of them are American. (There are Americans, and there are Japanese.)

blocks.instruction: Complete with 也, 都 or 常.

items.prompt: 陳先生喜歡喝茶，＿＿＿喜歡喝咖啡。

我不是日本人，他＿＿＿不是日本人。
我沒有哥哥，＿＿＿沒有姐姐。
他的家人都喜歡打網球，我家人也＿＿＿喜歡打網球。
我們＿＿＿不常踢足球。
我不＿＿＿游泳。

paras.text: Function: 吧 ba indicates a suggestion from the speaker.

a.zh: 我們去喝咖啡還是喝茶？
a.py: Wǒmen qù hē kāfēi háishì hē chá?
a.en: Shall we go drink coffee or tea?

a.zh: 今天晚上我們看什麼電影？
a.py: Jīntiān wǎnshàng wǒmen kàn shénme diànyǐng?
a.en: What movie are we watching tonight?

b.py: Wǒmen qù kàn Táiwān diànyǐng ba.

a.zh: 週末我們去打籃球，好不好？
a.py: Zhōumò wǒmen qù dǎ lánqiú, hǎo bù hǎo?
a.en: Let's go play basketball on the weekend, OK?

b.zh: 我不喜歡打籃球，我們打網球吧！
b.py: Wǒ bù xǐhuān dǎ lánqiú, wǒmen dǎ wǎngqiú ba!
b.en: I don't like to play basketball. Let's play tennis.

paras.text: Structures: 吧 ba is placed at the sentence-final position.
Usage: 吧 ba is used in imperatives to soften the command. For example, 喝吧。Hē ba. An imperative without 吧 ba sounds harsh and direct and can be impolite, for example, 喝！Hē!

blocks.en: III. Find What You Have in Common

paras.text: Goal: Learning to talk about what two people or groups of people have in common.
Task: Look at the chart below and try to discover what the people listed on it have in common. Do not repeat common points that somebody has already mentioned.
Example

items.zh: 我常喝咖啡，小王也常喝咖啡。
items.py: Wǒ cháng hē kāfēi, XiǎoWáng yě cháng hē kāfēi.
items.en: I often drink coffee. Xiao Wang also drinks coffee often.

items.zh: 我們和他弟弟都很常游泳。
items.py: Wǒmen hàn tā dìdi dōu hěn cháng yóuyǒng.
items.en: We and his brother often go swimming.

blocks.en: Bits of Chinese Culture — A One-of-a-kind Leisure Activity—Shrimp Fishing

paras.text: Shrimp fishing is a one-of-a-kind leisure activity found only in Taiwan. It is popular among locals and foreigners living in Taiwan and can be found on many travel itineraries for tourists.

The shrimp caught at shrimp-fishing sites are raised specifically for that purpose. The facilities are open to the public who is charged by the hour. Shrimp fishing originated in southern Taiwan in the 1980s and gradually spread to the rest of Taiwan. The first venues were outdoors, but shrimp fishing eventually became an indoor activity as enthusiasts wanted to stay out of the sun and weather. An indoor shrimp-fishing facility is a great place to spend half a day. You can roast the shrimp you catch or have them roasted by the staff and eat them right there.

There are many ways to cook shrimp, but nothing beats eating roasted shrimp and drinking beer. This laid-back leisure activity is a good way to relieve stress and a great escape from the hustle and bustle of daily life.

paras.text: Pinyin Rules
When the vowel “ü” is preceded by the consonant “j”, “q”, or “x,” the umlaut (the two dots above the letter) is omitted, e.g., jué (覺). When it is not preceded by any consonant, it is spelled yù (玉).
When the vowel “i” is followed by the vowel “a”, “o”, or “e” and is not preceded by consonant, change the “i” to a “y”, e.g., -iao → yào (要), -ie → yě (也).

blocks.en: Introduction to Chinese Characters — Using Components to Learn Chinese Characters

paras.text: Learning Chinese characters requires familiarizing yourself with their pronunciations, meanings, and form. The form (structure of Chinese characters) consists of structures with three tiers: the entire character itself, components, and strokes.
Components are the basic units of Chinese characters

Components are the smallest writing unit to Chinese characters. They fall between strokes and radicals (strokes ≦ components ≦ radicals) and are the core structures of Chinese writing. Independent characters have only one component and compound characters have at least two components. For example, the character in “好” has two components: “女” and “子.”
好＝女＋子
The character “樂” (happy) has three components: “白,” “幺,” and “木.”
樂＝白＋幺＋幺＋木
The most effective way to learn characters

Using components to learn Chinese characters helps the learner break down the complicated forms of characters and makes learning easier. Components also help the learner understand characteristics of Chinese characters and speeds up word recognition and learning, while helping build up word repertoire.
